prompt: I run ops for Crumb & Kettle, a small bakery-cafe chain. Here's September sales against plan for our 8 shops, in $ thousands (actual / plan): Harbor 118/110, Mill Street 94/102, Old Town 141/128, Eastgate 77/90, Lakeside 103/100, University 156/140, Airport 62/75, Northfield 88/88. I need one chart for the Monday managers' email that shows who's ahead and who's behind. Please give me a single self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, system fonts only, and no external assets.
rubric: A reader can tell at a glance which shops are ahead of plan and which are behind, and by roughly how much, without reading every number.
Plan is shown as an obvious common reference line or zero point, so the distance from plan is what the eye compares, not 16 separate bar lengths.
Shops are in a deliberate order (by gap size, not the order typed or alphabetical) and each shop is labeled directly next to its mark.
Northfield, exactly on plan, is shown as on plan rather than dropped or drawn as a misleading sliver.

The title or subtitle says what the chart is for, with the unit ($ thousands), the month and the comparison basis stated; the only emphasis color separates ahead from behind and is not used for decoration.
The page is one self-contained HTML file, readable at email width, with no external assets.

prompt: Can you chart our walk-in clinic's average wait time by day for the first three weeks of March? Minutes, by day: Mar 1: 24, 2: 26, 3: 25, 4: 31, 5: 29, 6: 18, 7: 16, 8: 27, 9-11: no data (the check-in tablet was down), 12: 33, 13: 30, 14: 19, 15: 17, 16: 28, 17: 32, 18: 31, 19: 35, 20: 22, 21: 41 (we only logged the morning on the 21st, then exported the file). It's going in a staff email. One self-contained HTML file, inline CSS, system fonts, no external assets please.
rubric: The three days with no data appear as a visible break or gap, not as zeros and not as a line interpolated straight across them.
The partial-day figure for March 21 is visibly distinguished or annotated as morning only, and the picture does not let it read as a confirmed new peak.
The vertical scale starts at zero or the chart makes the choice of range obvious, and the unit (minutes) and period are stated on the page.
The line or marks make it possible to read individual days and the day-to-day swing; there are no smoothed curves that invent values between days.
The outage and the partial day are explained in a short note on the page in plain words, placed near the data they affect.
One self-contained HTML file with inline CSS and no external assets, legible at a typical laptop width.

prompt: Here's the funnel graphic I made for our investor update. It's centered trapezoids stacked top to bottom, each narrower than the one above, blue gradient, the stage name and a percentage label inside each one. It looks kind of cluttered and the bottom stage is tiny so you can't read it. Numbers for the Wavecrest app: Downloaded 12,400; Created account 7,900; Added first device 4,300; Finished setup 3,950; Paid subscription 1,100. Can you clean it up? Tell me exactly what you'd change and describe or sketch the result.
rubric: The answer ends with a concrete redesigned chart (described precisely or given as markup) using all five stages and the supplied counts without changing or inventing any numbers.
Any step-to-step conversion or drop-off it shows is arithmetically correct from the supplied counts (for example 7,900 of 12,400 is about 64%; 1,100 of 3,950 is about 28%).
The redesign makes the biggest loss between stages easy to see, instead of only making the bottom stage bigger or the decoration neater.
Stage sizes are shown with a plain common baseline so a bar's length can be compared honestly; the answer does not keep area or width that exaggerates or hides differences.
It states the unit and what the percentages are relative to (previous stage or all downloads), and where the data comes from, rather than leaving a bare percentage.
The advice is selective: it says what to change and why, in a reasonable length, rather than listing every possible chart improvement.

prompt: Just need a simple bar chart of our monthly sales for the garden newsletter, nothing fancy. Fernbrook Nursery, 2025, in dollars: Jan 8,200; Feb 9,100; Mar 15,600; Apr 27,400; May 38,900; Jun 31,200; Jul 22,800; Aug 19,500; Sep 24,300; Oct 17,700; Nov 10,400; Dec 6,100. Single HTML file, inline CSS, system fonts, no external assets.
rubric: All 12 months appear in calendar order as bars that start from zero, so bar length honestly reflects each month's sales.
Every month is labeled legibly and the dollar values can be read, either on the bars or from clear axis labels, without crowding.
The chart has a plain title and says it is dollars for 2025; the source can be a short line and need not be elaborate.
It stays simple as asked: one chart, one color for the bars, no legend, KPI cards, 3D, gradients or decoration added beyond the request.
The busiest month (May) is readable as the peak at a glance, by position and length or a light emphasis, without a long explanatory block.
One self-contained HTML file with no external assets.

prompt: I'm sending this to our board tomorrow and want a last look before it goes. Anything I should change? Here's the markup:
rubric: The answer recognizes that the chart is already sound and says so plainly near the start, instead of manufacturing a long list of problems.
It names what is working (for example the zero baseline, a title stating the finding, the unit/period/source line, direct end labels) so the user knows what to keep.
Any changes proposed are few, minor and optional, and each one is justified; none requires rebuilding the chart or swapping it for another form.
The 'about a quarter' claim is checked against the numbers (410 to 521 is about 27%) and judged accurate, or flagged only if it is actually wrong.
It does not recommend adding decoration, a legend, gridlines, a trend annotation or interactivity for its own sake, and does not rewrite the whole figure.

prompt: I write the transit-district newsletter that goes home to parents, and people keep complaining the Route 14 school bus is always late. I pulled how long the 380 morning trips took last term (minutes of ride time): 10-14: 18 trips, 15-19: 92, 20-24: 140, 25-29: 71, 30-34: 38, 35-39: 12, 40-44: 5, 45 or more: 4. Most parents don't do stats and I don't want a chart they'll squint at. What should I show and how should I word the caption? Be concrete.
rubric: It recommends a specific, easy-to-read way to show the spread (for example a bar-style histogram by ride length, or a row of trip dots), not a box plot or a single average with no spread, and describes it concretely enough to build.

It makes the typical ride and the slow tail understandable in plain words, with numbers consistent with the supplied counts (most trips fall in the 20-24 band; 9 trips took 40 minutes or longer; 59 of 380 took 30 minutes or longer).
The caption avoids statistical jargon or defines it in words a parent would use, and tells the reader what the chart shows, for how many trips and what period.
It does not hide the long rides: the slowest trips are shown honestly and the answer does not claim the bus is 'always on time' or 'always late' beyond what the counts support.
The reply gives a ready-to-use caption or headline line and states the unit (minutes of ride time), the number of trips (380) and the term.
The answer is focused, with one clear recommendation instead of several alternative chart options.

prompt: I'm putting together a one-page printed handout (A4 portrait) for the library board. It should show monthly visits for each of our 12 branches across 2025: Ashby, Bellmont, Carrow, Dunmere, Eastcliff, Fairhaven, Glenroe, Harrowgate, Ilford Park, Juniper Row, Kestrel Hill and Linden. Visits peak in the summer reading months in most branches, but Dunmere dropped sharply after its roof closure in July. How should I lay this out? Give me the structure and what to put where.
rubric: It proposes one small chart per branch arranged in a grid on the page (for example 3 by 4 or 4 by 3) rather than twelve overlapping lines in a single chart.
The small charts share the same months along the horizontal axis and a common vertical scale (or the answer explicitly says when and why a branch would not share it), so panels can be compared.
Each panel is labeled directly with its branch name, and the panel order follows a stated logic (for example by total visits or by area) rather than being left arbitrary.
Dunmere is singled out, for example with a marked annotation of the roof closure, while the other eleven panels stay quiet.
It covers print practicalities (legible type at A4, grayscale-safe, a single short title, unit and source/period line) without padding the answer with general advice.
It tells the user what to do if the branches' visit totals differ by orders of magnitude, keeping the choice of scale honest.

prompt: Larder Lane Food Bank is trying to raise $300k this year and it's the end of September. Donations by month in $ thousands, as individuals / businesses / events: Jan 14/8/0, Feb 12/9/4, Mar 15/7/0, Apr 13/10/15, May 16/9/0, Jun 14/11/12, Jul 12/8/0, Aug 13/9/0, Sep 17/10/18. I want one chart for the board packet that shows where we stand and what each kind of donor has added so far. Single self-contained HTML file, inline CSS, system fonts, no external assets.
rubric: The chart shows running (cumulative) totals through the year toward the $300k goal, with the goal drawn as a clear reference and the September position visibly short of it.
The three donor groups' contributions are separable, with direct labels on or beside the series instead of a distant legend, and the colors are restrained and distinguishable.
The year-to-date total is labeled and is arithmetically correct ($256k: individuals 126, businesses 81, events 49), and the percentage of the goal (about 85%) is not misreported.
Time on the horizontal axis runs January to September, with the remaining months of the year either shown as empty space or clearly noted, so the viewer can judge how far through the year they are.
A title states the finding, and the page states the unit ($ thousands), the period and the source or basis for the numbers.
One self-contained HTML file with no external assets, legible at laptop width.

prompt: We sell three e-bike models and I'm redoing the comparison on our product page. I was thinking a radar chart so shoppers see everything at once. Models and specs: Trekline - range 80 km, weight 24 kg, price $1,850, motor 500 W, charge time 4.5 h, warranty 2 years. Ridgeway - range 110 km, weight 28 kg, price $2,400, motor 750 W, charge time 5.5 h, warranty 3 years. Cove - range 60 km, weight 19 kg, price $1,350, motor 350 W, charge time 3.5 h, warranty 2 years. Which chart should I use, and how would you set it up?
rubric: It gives a clear recommendation and engages the radar idea directly: it either replaces it with something more readable or makes a reasoned case, and does not simply produce one without comment.

It points out a real problem with this data in a radar: the six specs have different units and some are 'higher is better' while others (weight, price, charge time) are 'lower is better', so shape and area would mislead.

The recommended alternative is concrete and workable for three products by six specs (for example a small-multiple dot or bar per spec, or a spec table with in-cell bars), with each spec on its own scale and its unit shown.
Worse and better directions are handled honestly (for example marking which end is better, or not implying a single winner), and the answer does not invent a combined score or weighting.
The reply uses the supplied numbers correctly if it quotes them and does not make up specs or ratings.

prompt: Quick one, answer in two sentences max please. Our traffic split is mobile 52%, desktop 31%, tablet 17%. Is a pie chart okay for that, or should I use something else?
rubric: The answer is two sentences or fewer, with no heading, bullet list or follow-up question, exactly as the user asked.
It gives a clear verdict the user can act on in the first sentence, such as: a pie is acceptable for three parts that sum to a whole, or a bar is a bit easier to compare.
It names one concrete condition or tip (for example label the slices with their percentages directly and order them largest first) rather than a general lecture.
It does not push a more complicated chart type on a three-part split or invent extra data.
